utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's start from here. Accused Miletic is absent today. We have received the waiver signed by him. Otherwise, all the other accused are present. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer. From the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Ms. Nikolic and Mr. Haynes. Right. Mr. Ostojic, we heard you wished to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. I would just like to inform the Court of the scheduling issues that we are dealing with and to ask for some assistance and guidance from the Court. I think we've resolved it. I've spoken to my learned friends. They're in agreement, but I do need the Court to make sure that you accept it as well. First, if I can address the witness 2DW83, which is a DutchBat person. His schedule is very complicated in the sense that he is still working, and from our contacts with him he can only meet with me next Thursday or Friday and then possibly testify the following week. He's in Germany and is travelling with respect to his schedule. We were hoping to bring him in in the last week of our case and hoping to end by the 12th of September, and as I go on I think it will make much clearer sense to the Court. Secondly, if I may proceed, it was with respect to witness 2DW41. Last night -- he's the witness which the Court gave us the right to take a videolink in Belgrade next week. We scheduled it. We thought he was going to be live. We had set him for last week and this week. His family called our staff and was very concerned that his health is ill. We spoke with our client, and he agreed that our recommendation, that we will withdraw him if the Court permits. Again, that's why we are raising it with the Court. We've advised our learned friends of that, as well, and they don't have an objection, I believe, to that, either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was going to be the 9th, correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then moving along to another perhaps complicated issue is 2DW50. We've tried, and as you may recall, our lead investigator in Belgrade has suffered a very serious eye disease, and he's getting treatment, and therefore, we withdrew him as well. But he was also in contact with 2DW50, whom I've met with in the past. We're not establishing contact with this witness. We may be asking the Court either to subpoena the witness or to assist us to bring him in or to have his interview with the OTP be presented pursuant to 92 quarter. We haven't thought it all out, but I'm just advising the Court of that because he seems to be unavailable to us at least. I know 92 Court order addresses deceased, but the rule is general that it states that it is actually for the unavailability --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for the interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And he's the driver, if the Court recalls. 2DW50. Speaking of 92 quarter, we're going to present -- and I've spoken with the lawyer of witness 2DW82 who's -- who I've spoken to on two occasions, and he was a former accused who is serving his sentence. We prepared an affidavit for him to sign. He became ill thereafter, and his lawyer says because they do not have a decision on his contempt case that he is not going to testify and they're not recommending that he testify. I've lost contact with him since he became ill, but I have my notes and the two draft statements that we were going to have him execute for us, which were unexecuted, but he made changes from one to another one, and what we're hoping to present that -- we hope to file that no later than Friday for the Court and also with respect to witness 2DW79 who is the elder --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the Interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: 2DW79 which is the journalist from Arizona in the United States. I did speak to him a couple of times, and we have his diary as the Court knows. We're going to be asking, also, that that be admitted pursuant to 92 quater. With respect to the next witness, it's 2DW100, again, a journalist. He gave a statement to the OTP, which we moved earlier to be presented pursuant to 92 quarter in some of our filings. The Prosecution objected and said they wanted us to obtain a death certificate from him. We are in the process of procuring that death certificate. It was complicated because we did not know where he died and where they would have filed such a certificate. Our information from some other people that were in contact with us is that they should be able to get that death certificate if necessary within the next two weeks, so I just wanted to advise the Court on that. And then with respect to the next witness I would ask that we move into close session, if we may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's... [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And I've spoken with my learned friends, and they are in agreement, if the Court approves it, of course, so we would propose for this week that we continue with the witness that's currently on the stand, 2DW5, Mr. Mitrovic. But we would ask the Court not to proceed with the next witness that we have scheduled, which was 2DW77, and one of the main reasons is because we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wasn't the next witness going to be -- because you keep referring to the next witness, and each time the name of the next witness changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We -- I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And instead of clarifying things, I can assure you that quite exceptionally, I feel rather confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, and I apologise for that. I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: --thinking why I'm unable to follow or whether you are confusing the issue. I don't know. But in my opinion, the next one was going to be 2DW608.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did speak with the Prosecution in connection with that, and the problem is that Mr. Srdja Trifkovic can only testify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not Trifkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I know that -- I know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, it's Wagenaar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I know that. Mr. Srdja Trifkovic can only testify Thursday and Friday. We didn't want there to be a three-time interruption with Professor Wagenaar if he starts today. Then we would have to bring him back Friday part-time because that -- based on the estimates Srdja Trifkovic may take a day and a half and then have to bring him back Monday. I've spoken to him. He's not staying at a hotel because he lives approximately two hours outside of The Hague and he feels more comfortable sleeping in his own house with his family, so -- but he is going to drive. We're trying to reduce that. With respect to that, my friends have agreed that we start Mr. Wagenaar on Friday immediately after Mr. Trifkovic and then proceed with him on Monday and as long as it takes, but they do -- they have estimated approximately three hours for him as well. So we were going to start with Mr. Trifkovic tomorrow and end with him on Friday and then proceed with Professor Wagenaar on Friday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what are we going to do today apart from Mr. Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I would propose that, unfortunately, we leave early, Mr. President, if that's acceptable or possible. If it's not, as I've told my learned friends, I'm prepared to proceed with Professor Wagenaar. He --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but is he here?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: He is here, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, he's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I met with him this morning. I just think that it might be unreasonable to have him come three instead of two days given his schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are here to work. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The agreement is that we continue with Mitrovic, and then we start with Professor Wagenaar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That leads us to the next week, Mr. President. I think then we may have a problem with Tuesday, just so the Court is aware, and that's why I was suggesting if I complete the schedule, it seems to fit so we don't have a gap for next week. And I'm not sure how long we have left with Mr. Mitrovic, but if we -- and with all due respect, we're prepared to proceed, and I know it's valuable Court time, but the schedule, it occurred because of one person's ill health and a change with respect to the Washington lawyer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That, I understand, Mr. -- however, let's put things -- make things clear. You have mentioned the possibility or the probability of filings under rule -- under one rule or the other but particularly 92 quarter or -- or 94. I don't which section you mentioned. In any case, please, if you have to file, do proceed straightaway so that we know exactly and you know exactly where everyone stands because time is of the essence here. That's number one. Secondly, as for Tuesday of next week when that witness will not be testifying anymore by videolink, we have to find a substitution. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's why we had 2DW55, but the Court ordered him to start on Wednesday and Thursday. The other witnesses are scheduled to arrive on Monday, and I don't know exactly the time. If we can get them Tuesday, we'll bring them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If Professor Wagenaar -- what I remember, you require him for practically one whole day.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right? The Prosecution also practically require him for another day, so -- and then the Nikolic team require one hour, for example. So we are basically talking of two days for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have that set for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So he is going to testify starting today. Then tomorrow and Friday, it's going to be Trifkovic or whatever his name is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then Monday, we continue with the professor, which will bring us into Tuesday because he won't have the full three and a half hours that you have asked for him today.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so the Court's aware of it, if we come up short next week I just want you to be aware of it. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but can't you have one of the witnesses that are arriving on Monday ready to testify on Tuesday?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll try our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Then, Mr. President, the other issue is we are waiting to receive a diary or an appointment diary of Radovan Karadzic which was seized during his arrest. We got an e-mail today that they were going to produce that for us today. It may be relevant to Srdja Trifkovic's testimony tomorrow, so we would hope that we get that so we would have an opportunity to review it tonight, I guess, or whenever we get it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are not summoning Mr. Karadzic, however?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't think so. All right. Do you wish to comment, Mr. McCloskey or Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We'll proceed and then make adjustments as necessary, as they may become necessary. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, judges and colleagues. Just to let you know, Mr. President, we did have a meeting with the victims and witness's section yesterday, so as mentioned previously we are ready to go with the case for the Defence of Drago Nikolic. However, we do need a date before the motion, the -- we can get things in motion to get the first witnesses to arrive to The Hague, so it will be important for us to have a starting date. And I'd also take this opportunity to mention that with regards to the cross-examination with the Professor Wagenaar, we should be shorter than the one hour which was put on our estimated time. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for that, Mr. Bourgon. All right. How much more time do you require for your cross-examination of Mr. Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think I need the second hour of my two-hour estimate for this witness. So it would be a full hour, I would say, at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. No, no, no. I just wanted to know more or less where we stand. Anything else? Madam usher, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Mitrovic. Welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you and good afternoon to you, too, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are still testifying under oath as per your solemn declaration yesterday. Mr. Thayer will proceed with his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When we broke yesterday we were talking about Colonel Beara's relationships with General Tolimir and General Mladic. May we have 65 ter 3516 on e-court, please. I just want to draw your attention to one paragraph on the seventh page of the B/C/S and the second page of the English, and I just want to ask you one question about this document. I think as I mentioned yesterday, this was seized from the Croatian Ministry of Defence in 1998. Do you see the document in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It says: "During August 1992, Beara was released from the prison when General Ratko Mladic and Zdravko Tolimir came personally to pick him up. Mladic and Zdravko Tolimir graduated together at the war school in Belgrade, and Zdravko Tolimir was deputy chief of the Split counterintelligence group before the war and the chief of the intelligence in the JNA Knin corps." My question to you, sir, is simply with respect to this statement here that Generals Mladic and Tolimir personally picked up Colonel Beara in August of 1992 upon his release from prison. Do you know anything about that occasion that you can share with the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've never heard of this before. So far I didn't know that General Mladic and General Tolimir personally went to pick up the Colonel from prison -- actually, for Naval Captain Beara. So far I didn't know that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during the war, based on your service in the security and intelligence field, you were able to see that General Tolimir valued Colonel Beara's work, did he not?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only provide you with my subjective opinion. I believe that Tolimir obviously valued Naval Captain Beara's work and that they held each other in a rather high esteem. That's what I can say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we may have 65 ter 3659, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And Mr. President, we'll need to go into closed session for the broadcast of this document and this discussion, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's do that. One moment. Yes, we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just a couple more follow-up questions, sir, on this issue of the conflict. Now, in addition to this name-calling that we've spoken about, the conflict also had a dimension, did it not, of one of the personalities of President Karadzic on the one hand as Supreme Commander and General Mladic on the other as the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In very simplified terms, you may say so because Karadzic was the leader of the civilian authorities and General Mladic was the leader of the military -- structure of the military organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And it was natural, was it not, then, for those closest to General Mladic also to come in for that type of criticism and abuse from the political leadership that General Mladic was the focus of?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, when we are talking about people's names, of the people surrounding General Mladic and General Mladic himself, they never spoke openly in the public about these names because that would have been counterproductive, I suppose. People, after all, supported the army throughout the war, but I suppose that when they mentioned Mladic they implied the entire Main Staff and all of his associates.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, from your knowledge, sir, General Mladic also valued Colonel Beara's work and trusted him as well. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say this is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It almost goes without saying that the commander of the Main Staff must trust his intelligence and security assistant commanders deeply, correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, a true commander who has a good security organ considers that security organ his right hand, his second in command. There were obviously different commanders and different security organs, of course. In any case, there was a high degree of mutual trust between the two. For example, I personally never had any problems in communicating with my corps commander. We always understood each other well, and I always had his support when it came to my duties and my part of the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Colonel, as far as you know, General Mladic never lost that trust in Colonel Beara during the war, did he?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think he lost that trust. If he had, then I suppose that Naval Captain Beara would have been removed from his position and replaced. And if you will allow me, I would also like to say that I need to apologise to the Trial Chamber, to yourself, and to the Defence. Yesterday I did not say that Naval Captain Beara some two or three years prior to the beginning of the war in Croatia was the chief of the security department in the naval district. I did not want to omit that deliberately, and I did not want to raise anybody's suspicion that I was covering things up. This is a generally known fact, that he was appointed chief and that he remained in that position until the beginning of the war and that he remained at that position until the moment he joined the Army of Republika Srpska. I hope you will take this into consideration and that you will accept my apology for not having mentioned that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, just speaking for the Prosecution, if that's your greatest infraction, you're are way ahead of the rest of us. Now, to your knowledge, sir, did General Mladic ever lose that trust in Colonel Beara after the war ended?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a shake-up after the war. All the men in the Main Staff were removed from their position; the General Staff of the Army Republika Srpska was established; and a new person, General Coric [phoen], became the chief of the General Staff; then General Savcic became the chief of the security administration. In other words, all the people who were in the leading positions during the war were removed from their positions after the war. There was a general shake-up in the structure of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If we may have 65 ter 3515, please, and we will be looking at pages 3 of both the English and the B/C/S with respect to this document. If we could just hang on to page 1 - I'm sorry - for just a moment, so we can acquaint the witness with it. Sir, this is a letter from General Manojlo Milovanovic that he wrote on September 29th, 2004, to the government of the Republika Srpska, and it has to do with a number of topics that he was addressing them on, including the whereabouts of the Main Staff archives and some other issues. What I'd like to do is turn your attention to just one portion of the paragraph on page 3 as I mentioned before, please. Do you see the paragraph that begins: "At the beginning of 1997, the then-acting president of the republic, Mrs. Biljana Plavsic, made a rash decision..." Do you see that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. General Milovanovic refers to the decision to relocate the new General Staff. I think that's what you were just referring to a moment ago. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. At that time, the General Staff was moved to the Bijeljina and from there it was moved to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Then it goes on further: "...and retire four generals from the former Main Staff, one of whom was General Djordje Djukic, who died eight months before his 'retirement' after being maltreated in prison in The Hague." Do you recall, Colonel, who the other three generals were that were retired?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, I remember the event like I told you. The complete war staff was removed from their positions. President Plavsic set up a completely new leadership. I don't remember which three generals were pensioned off. If we are talking about 1997, that was a power struggle and a little puch that Biljana Plavsic staged in order to get rid of Krajisnik and the others. I must say that when the war began I was major, and when the war ended I was lieutenant-colonel. After the war, I was a small fry, to put it that way, so I didn't know what was happening in the office of the president or what General Milovanovic wrote in any of his documents. And as for this document, I never saw it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If we read on, it says that: "General Mladic and I put ourselves at the disposal of the VRS for up to six months and for the other six months to the Yugoslav Army." So that's about a year. We're talking about here -- at the beginning of 1997, there's a reference, and then sometime after that we're talking about a year. My first question is, you served as assistant Minister of Defence under General Milovanovic from, I think, 1998 to 2001. My question is, if we read on it says that: "General Mladic stayed in Crna Rijeka with his security guards who were supposed to protect him from being arrested by The Hague Tribunal. Biljana Plavsic signed a decree about this. In the beginning the commander of that powerful security group was Colonel Ljubisa Beara because Mladic wished it so then it was Colonel and later Dragan Lalovic also because Mladic wished it so." Do you know anything about this topic, this statement that General Mladic wanted Colonel Beara to be in charge of his personal bodyguard protection team after he was indicted by The Hague? Do you know anything about that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know about it in the sense that this Colonel Lalovic was at the then-security of General Mladic, but I didn't know that General Mladic ever asked for Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So by the time you arrived, is what you're telling the Court that Mr. Lalovic was in charge, as the letter says?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't -- well, as a matter of fact, I didn't understand what you were asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just go back --

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand. My arrival, Lalovic's arrival, I'm not sure. I had no money in the game.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Your previous answer was: "I know about it in the sense that this Colonel Lalovic was at the then-security of General Mladic, but I didn't know that General Mladic ever asked for Colonel Beara." So my question to you, sir, was, by the time you showed up at the ministry of Defence in 1998, what you're telling the Trial Chamber is that at that time it was Colonel Lalovic as far as you knew who was in charge of the protection detail or group for General Mladic as it says here in the letter?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, may we have - and I'd like to turn to a different subject now - 65 ter 3661, please. While we're waiting for it to come up, I can tell you that it's going to be an order for further operations from the commander of the 2nd Krajina Corps. You were shown this document during your 2004 interview in Banja Luka. It's an 8 June 1992 order for further operations. Do you see the document in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, and it was shown to me during the interview in 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And if we just quickly go to page 5 of the English and page 4 of the B/C/S, we can see at paragraph 8 where there's the section on intelligence and security measures, it's divided into paragraph A, intelligence measures, and paragraph B, security measures, and the security measures continue onto page 5 of the B/C/S; both are paragraph 8. And then there's another section; if we go to page 7 of the English and page 6 of the B/C/S that discusses rear security, and I'll just give you a moment to look at that section on rear security. Does this help refresh your recollection about being shown this document in Banja Luka, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I'm not going to ask you questions so much about the military objectives or so forth that are contained in this order. I'm more interested in what you told us about the process that was involved. You said at pages 55 to 56 of your interview, and I'll just save some time and read this short passage, I quote: "The introduction of an order such as this is probably from a directive or an order by the Main Staff because it speaks about a wider area and the situation on the territory outside of the area of responsibility of the corps. An order like this would have been approved by the Main Staff before it was actually initiated." After you have a chance to process the translation, sir, do you have anything to add or change to that answer that you gave in 2004, and if not, I'll move on to a related topic.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing to add or take away, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we may have 65 ter 3625, please. You also spoke during your interview about your knowledge of the process by which the Main Staff passed on operational directives, and I'll just wait until we have both the English and the -- okay. Well -- okay. We have a translation in your own language of this portion that I wish to read to you. At page 37, y ou were asked the following question: "How does the Main Staff take and transform political strategic objectives into military operational directives to go to the corps? How does that happen?" Now, your answer was quite detailed, so as I said we have this B/C/S transcript for you of the section of your interview to read along. You said, and this begins at page 37 of the English, line 31: "I don't know these directives, but like any other member of the command I was informed of their content. But if you will allow me, I cannot remember the contents of these directives because it has been 12 years. The way to transform the decision of a political leadership into a military directive is the following. I'm giving an example..." And you say: "For instance, you've mentioned here the establishment of borders on the rivers Una and Neretva, which basically means that the 1st Krajina Corps and the 2nd Krajina Corps were issued with tasks or directives to establish a border, or in other words, positions on those two rivers, and if the positions are not already there, then the unit is issued with the task to plan to capture those positions to take those positions. And it's up to the corps command to device the combat operation in order to fulfill this directive. And this means that the Herzegovina corps would be issued with the task for the River Neretva and so on. So for the corridor it would be the east Bosnian and the 1st corps and so on." Now, sir, there you're referring to one of the six strategic objectives issued by the Republika Srpska National Assembly on 12 May 1992. You were shown that during your interview, and that particular strategic objective number 4 called for establishing a border on the Una and Neretva rivers. Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, just picking up in the English, it's page 38 and line 15, and if you can continue along, you were asked the question: "If I have it kind of right here, the Main Staff then sets the big picture based on strategic goals and gives the corps commander certain tasks to carry out but leaves the corps commander with the authority to get that done in the best way that he sees fit?" And your answer was: "So, yes, you see, the Main Staff was the strategic command. And it gives global tasks which are in accordance with the decisions made by the political representatives with the policies. Because the politics governed us, as it did many other armies. So, it's usually the way that in the introductions to the directive, you're given an overview or a dissection of the overall combat situation on the territory of the entire VRS. They probably referred to this decision of the assembly as well. I don't know whether there were any orders by the Supreme Commander or the Supreme Command in the war, and if there is an order issued by the Supreme Command, then the Main Staff invokes that order. So basically, what they're doing is they're creating the widest possible foundation or basis. And as you go further down the levels, the tasks narrow down and they become more and more concrete. Because if they issued the 2nd Krajina Corps with the task to come out on the banks of the Una River, then this must have been, like, one or two sentences at the most. And now the 2nd Krajina Corps command assesses the task. They assess their own manpower, forces, and positions, the combat positions that they know where they are and what they are. They assess the enemy forces, and through that comes into life the decision-making process, and the decision is made on the use of the units in order to fulfill the task that was issued through that directive. The decision is made and signed by the corps commander because he's the exclusive one who is in charge of that. That's what makes him the commander. And this decision, this order for the use of the units is then sent to the lower-ranking units which in our case were the brigades or regiments because we didn't have any other. So when a brigade receives such an order, such a decision, such a task for the carrying out of combat activities, then they make their own; then they issue their own order decision -- order or decision because - how should I say this - the corps order is a bit -- is a bit rough for them." There's some further discussion, and you are asked the question -- this is at page 39, line 24. The question posed to you by the investigator was: "So the task gets more specific as you go down this funnel that you described from global?" And you answer: "More concrete, yes." You're asked the follow-up question: "From global directives to operational directives, to brigade-level combat operations orders down to the very platoon that's actually -- take that hill?" And your answer, and I'm just going to read this last portion and then follow up with a question: "Yes. Yes, you've got two trenches here, three, and that's what you do, and it all has to be, of course, synchronized because the brigade has to submit its decision to the corps command for inspection, and the commander of the corps has to approve their decision because they have to stand up and fight for their -- defend their decision. And it was the same with the corps command. They had to send their decision to the Main Staff for approval, so it was like a reverse process." Now, sir, when you said "reverse process" during your interview, can you tell the Trial Chamber what you meant by there was a reverse process?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, first and foremost, when I said "reverse process," I meant, for example, when a brigade makes its decision on the operation of its forces, the commander needs to defend that decision before the corps commander and before the corps command, either the staff or command. In any case, the commander has to hear him out and needs to approve of his decision. Once all brigade decisions have come in, all of the brigade commanders need to come in to defend them, and only after the process the brigade commanders can call up meetings and issue orders to battalion commanders and then further down the chain to companies and so on. The same goes for the corps commander. Once it has all been dealt with at the brigade levels, the decision made by the corps commander on its operation needs to go to the Main Staff to take personally that decision there and argue in its favour before the Main Staff commander for him to approve it. That's roughly put. You've read out quite a lot, but that's the decision-making process, or rather, drafting orders and directives of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, let me just read to you one more portion, a short paragraph on page 40 of the English, and this is also in the B/C/S translation before you. You said at line 14: "This whole decision-making process of the lower levels cannot even begin without the Main Staff approving the decision of the corps commander. Only when the Main Staff approves the decision of the corps command can they then start formulating the decisions, the orders to the brigades and the lower commands. In the same fashion, the brigade cannot order anything to the battalions without the corps command having approved it." That's basically what you just told us a moment ago, sir. Now, you continue on: "What you ask issue is a preparatory order, which basically means that you withdraw people, you bring people back from leave, that you increase the supply of ammunition, increase the supply of food and other combat necessities. So these are the first indications whereby you know that something important is underway." Is a preparatory order, Colonel, sometimes referred to as a warning order, or are those interchangeable -- or are those different things?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You put it correctly. There were preparatory orders. Occasionally, they were put in writing. Such a preparatory order can include tasks for units to prepare for the forthcoming tasks. Such tasks in my understanding are roughly described only in such preparatory orders. The preparatory orders can encompass a number of measures and activities that a certain unit needs to take in order to raise its combat-readiness to as high a degree as possible in order to be ready to fulfill its ensuing tasks. I don't know whether there's any particular time specified in a preparatory order. I can't tell you that. I'm not an expert in that area. As a matter of fact, I've also mentioned some of the elements of particular interest for security people when they want to see if there was something going on, if there are any preparations. All these elements have to be gone through for a unit to be prepared in the best possible way for any future tasks. This includes reconnaissance at all levels, and there's also something that we call command reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. In your experience, sir, do those preparatory orders require Main Staff approval, or are those orders something that can be issued by the corps by itself; in other words, if the Main Staff was happy to leave that in the hands of the corps without having to sign off on it?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my opinion that the Main Staff also issued such preparatory orders. I cannot be 100-percent certain, but I can presume that most likely it was done. There were preparatory orders issued to the effect that some military operations were to take place. Staff officers could tell you more about the process of everything you've been asking me. In any case, I think there were such preparatory orders in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at your level, Colonel, at the corps level, just based on your experience, when the corps issued a preparatory order, was that something that had to be approved by the Main Staff, or did the corps have the authority to begin issuing such preparatory orders by itself?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if a corps receives a preparatory order from the Main Staff, then they issue their preparatory order at their level and send it down to the brigades. I don't think they needed any special approval for that. A preparatory order in my view includes the corps being familiarized with the task, and then in turn it has to draft a preparatory order at its level for its subordinate units, much as would be the case with combat orders. After having received an order from the Main Staff, they no longer needed any special permission to send to down the channel -- the chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, this may seem like an obvious question, but as a member of the corps command, although you said you can't recite the number of directives that were passed on to the corps by the Main Staff or maybe the subject matter of each and every one of those directives, at the time you would have -- and you were informed of their content; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of the interview, I said something that I will repeat now. I wasn't familiar with it, and I don't know what the number of such directives was. I don't know, but I can presume that not all directives necessarily had to do with the same part of territory. They may have been wider or narrower in scope, but I don't know that. What I do know is that those directives that had to do with the area of responsibility of the corps, as a command member I was familiar with their contents and the tasks that the corps units were to implement. This would usually include the whole corps staff and command. They would meet and the corps commander would read out the directive, familiarizing us with its contents. Then we would go on to discuss how we could implement that directive the best way possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, when we speak of a corps-wide operation such as the one we looked at a few moments ago, that order for further operations from June of 1992, prior to such an operation there will be security and intelligence assessments made by the corps command in connection with that operation. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is customary in the work of commands that such assessments are made and security and intelligence support needed to be provided as separate items in any orders. The intelligence organ was supposed to provide any information they had about the enemy and their posts, and pursuant to that data, decisions were made on how to deploy units, which axis to engage, which would be the main units to implement the tasks, and so on and so forth. The security organs were supposed to provide an overview of the security situation in the corps territory. As I was saying then, intelligence personnel covered from the point of contact between us and the enemy and then into enemy territory in depth, whereas security or counterintelligence organs focused their activities on the area of the corps itself. We provided elements that had to do with intelligence, security support by way of an attachment. It was one of the tasks of the security organ. We would provide that attachment that was supposed to corroborate the item of any particular order that had to do with intelligence and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this important security and intelligence information, this is both coming up from the subordinate units and taking yourself as a member of the corps command staff. It's coming up to you, but it's also coming down to you from the Main Staff security administration because it is receiving similar information from other corps which might impact on your corps' activity; is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. This is how our information system worked. The information was conveyed from the reconnaissance platoons in the brigade, would be delivered to the corps command, and as for us, we collected intelligence every day and we would convey this intelligence to the security and intelligence sector. And every day in return we would receive from them information and intelligence that provided us with the entire picture of the events in the entire territory of Republika Srpska as well as the information that contained elements relative to the zone of responsibility of our corps. If there was such information, then we would use it to devise our plans of operation. Let me just add to that that the intelligence that we see from the Main Staff was discussed at every corps command meeting. First, the intelligence would be read out loud and then discussed. In other words, everybody was made aware of what the intelligence was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And because of the importance of this information, this is one reason why the corps could not withhold any intelligence or security-related matter from General Tolimir. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We couldn't do that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In fact, when you were asked the following question during your interview -- let me just read it to you. It's from page 95 of the English: "Is there any reason you can think of where there would be any secrets from General Tolimir, any intelligence or security-related matter?" You answered: "In my case, there definitely wasn't any. I can't tell you anything about other organs, but in principle there shouldn't have been any because, also, General Tolimir would have surely found out if something had been kept a secret. And in that case, I wouldn't like to be in the skin of the person who tried to keep secrets from him." Do you have anything to add or change or subtract, as you said, from your answer, or do you stand with that today as well?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not wish to add or underline anything with regard to the answer that you have just read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I want to move to a different area. You referred yesterday during your testimony - and this is at page 25071 - to an occasion when your commander told you to prevent units from deserting their positions, and you told the Trial Chamber that that wasn't your responsibility and that was an example that you gave of how things weren't working properly in your field. You referred to: "The commander would often go and tell me to bring back a unit from its position or try to -- and prevent people running away from their positions or to go and disarm paramilitary units if they turned up." And we'll talk about paramilitary units a little later, but with respect to this issue of soldiers deserting their positions, if it wasn't your responsibility, whose responsibility was it to make sure that soldiers weren't deserting their units and maintain their will to fight?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First and foremost, this would be the responsibility of the commanders and commandeers of these units because they were the supreme organs of security in their respective units and in charge of the morale of the -- in those particular units. Depending on the ability the commander to raise the morale of his people to stay in positions and to fight, depending on their abilities and their personal example, their -- the situations varied. Some were able to do that, and therefore, there were units that never abandoned their positions because the system of command and control was good. But there were also other cases where the system of control and command was not so good, and there were frequent cases of desertion. I had a situation that a complete brigade abandoned the positions. They were resubordinated to us. I went to their positions, and I saw that their commander was actually leading them, and there was nothing I could do. To cut a long story short, where the command and control was functioning well and where the commander was in charge and had the authority over his soldiers, there was no wilful abandonment of the frontlines by the troops. Where the system was impaired, there were obviously very frequent instances of desertion. It was even a wide-scale phenomenon in some units.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see we're getting near the break. I'm about to start a substantive area with some documents. If we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought you were going to tell us you were about to finish. You've gone, I think, beyond your two hours that you had asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I have, Mr. President. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I would suggest that you try and cut it down and conclude, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I will do that over the break, Mr. President. I will need a little bit more time with the Court's permission. It's moving a little slower than I had estimated through these important areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I will put "important" in inverted commas. Let's have the break now, 25 minutes, and in the meantime, please, if you could work out for us the time that Mr. Thayer has been cross-examining this witness. Thank you. --- Break taken at is 3.40 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, I read to you in connection with your testimony about the process of translating the Main Staff, the directives the Main Staff passed on into concrete military action. I read to you a long portion of your statement that you read along as well. I just want to first ask you, do you stand by what you said to the investigators in 2004?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, let me move on quickly, my last couple of questions. You said in your OTP interview, also, that the state of combat morale is extremely important within a fighting unit. Can you describe for the Trial Chamber the importance of cooperation between the morale organs and the security and intelligence organs?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to clarify some things. Actually, I would like to say that both the security organ and the assistant for morale are members of the same team, and obviously, there must be cooperation among the team members. People obviously have to communicate and exchange information among themselves. They are almost duty-bound to do that within the command. It is common practice, if that answers your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And why was it important to have that communication between the morale organs and the organs for security and intelligence?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to understand this question, one has to say that during the process of assessing the state of morale in a unit, a lot of elements have to be analysed as having impact on the state of morale. One of them is security or the security threats. One of those is obviously desertions, abandoning positions, throwing up weapons. All these are forms of behaviour that have a negative impact on the status of morale, which have to be taken into consideration. It is common practice to have meetings of the command where everybody provides information pertinent to their respective sectors and shares problems from their own domain, and this is the first instance at which the information on the problems in the unit are exchanged. One of those problems has to do with the state of morale in that unit. I don't know whether I've made myself clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say, Colonel, that the security situation affects the morale, and the morale situation affects the security situation?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A correlation of that sort may be taken into account. In practice, that was the case, and of course, you can also put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, again, just taking you directly to your 2004 interview. You were asked the following question at page 102: "We've talked about General Milan Gvero before, chief of morale, religious and legal affairs. Now, he issued thousands of reports about the current political situation. Now, much of what is in your report is also of political nature, so were there times when you would read General Gvero's reports and extract part of those that you felt relevant for the intelligence report?" And your answer was: "I don't exclude such a possibility. It depended on the character of information we were drafting. It depended on its contents and the goal that we had that we wanted to achieve with that information. I believe, and I know, that General Gvero and Tolimir cooperated very closely, so I don't exclude the possibility that in his reports Gvero would use Tolimir's information and Tolimir, Gvero's, and they would basically fill in the gaps." Do you stand by that answer that you gave in Banja Luka, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, just two quick final questions, sir. You referred to paramilitaries at one point in one of your answers that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could my learned friend read the next question and answer. We suggest that that is out of context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Thayer, do you have comments to that? In the meantime, for the record, the Prosecution, I also notice the presence of Mr. Nicholls, and Ms. Nikolic has been present in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I certainly can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Question: "Can I -- can I just ask you what kind -- what kind of officer Gvero was? Did you know him very well?" And your answer was: "I didn't know him very well. I knew him. I met him during the war when he used to come to the corps, the corps' area of responsibility. I know he is from Mrkonjic Grad, and I know that before the war he was the spokesperson of the SSNO and that he practically spent his entire time serving in Belgrade, and when I was telling you yesterday about my imprisonment he is the person who couldn't provide my father with an answer of where I was. He was a very educated officer."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you mentioned paramilitaries the other day, and when you were asked about this in Banja Luka, you said, and this is page 126: "So basically, you had to make a compromise. It's better to keep them under your wing, put them into the army, have them fight for you and keep them under control than to have them as loose cannons." Is it correct, therefore, to say that in some cases the VRS had to forcibly remove paramilitaries but in others they were able to convince the paramilitaries to join you and work towards a common cause?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right. During the war, and I'm talking about the zone of responsibility of my corps, at the beginning of the war, actually, different groups arrived allegedly wanting to fight together with the Serbian people, but they had different criminal agenda. All the groups that would not be placed under the command of the army or in the specific case of the corps were disarmed and expelled from the zone of responsibility of my corps. They arrived in different ways, through different channels, but all those who would not be placed under our command had to leave our zone of responsibility. When you were talking about a compromise, you were talking about one specific case of a unit from the 1st Krajina Corps, which had started out by acting as an independent paramilitary unit from Vucak, I believe. And subsequently, they were incorporated into the army and became a regular unit of the 1st Krajina Corps, although their commander had been convicted for a crime before the war, and hence my second example of compromises that had to be made during the war to accommodate such groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Understood, Colonel. Last topic, briefly. Going back to the world that existed when you were serving in the JNA, under the rules and under the practice adhered to by the JNA while it still existed, what would happen to a soldier or an officer who openly displayed ethnic hatred or intolerance or hostility towards a co-worker?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Talking about the time the JNA existed in the former Yugoslavia, that was considered a crime. Any such person - be it a soldier or an officer or even a commissioned officer; it really did not make any difference - any such person would be subject to measures prescribed by law.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what would happen to a soldier or an officer who openly voiced nationalistic sentiments while they were serving in the JNA, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such persons would be subject to measures prescribed by law because any display of ethnic hatred in the JNA - which was the epitome of brotherhood and unity at the time - was considered a crime, and that's why such persons would be prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Punishable by what, sir? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean, sir. In any case, depending on the gravity of the crime that they committed; it depended whether they acted independently, whether they acted on their own or in concert with somebody else, whether they were members of an organised illegal group, whether they inflicted damage upon the image of the JNA. It all depended on the judiciary, and the judiciary decided the type of punishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. That concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Re-examination, but before that, I notice Mr. Bourgon standing. Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I would like to have special permission by the Court to ask one question, one further question in cross-examination, which arises with the questions that have been put by my colleague from the Prosecution to the witness. If the witness can take his earphone, I will gladly share this question with the Court in order to get the proper leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's your knowledge of English like, Mr. Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] None whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay, could you remove your headphones for awhile, please. Yes, Mr. Bourgon. What's the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The question reads as follows, and I will read the exact question in the transcript so I can get you to consider. My colleague from the Prosecution asked you many questions concerning the issuing of orders from the Main Staff to the corps level to the brigades as well as questions relating to what is known in western armies as the back-briefing process when orders are issued. I have only one question for you in this regard, which goes as follows: On the basis of your military experience, can you think of any order involving the implementation of activities which require the use of resources which could be issued by a corps to one of the assistant commanders in a brigade without first informing the Brigade commander? That is the question, Mr. President, and this question arises from questions that have been put by my colleague to the witness, questions which -- the aim of which was to obtain evidence favourable to its own case and which were not related to the reason for which this witness is here in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And is there re-examination, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will have brief re-examination. A couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we decide on Mr. Bourgon's request, Mr. Thayer, do you wish to comment or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have no objection to the question being asked exceptionally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So our decision is to allow the question always on the proviso that the witness can answer it because it may well be that he cannot. But Mr. Mitrovic, there is a further question for you from the Defence team of Mr. Nikolic. See if you can understand it and answer it. If you can't answer it, please let us know. Go ahead, Mr. Bourgon. Read it out slowly for the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My colleague from the Prosecution asked you many questions concerning the issuing of orders from the Main Staff to the corps level to the brigades as well as questions relating to what is known in western armies as "the back-briefing process" when orders are issued. I only have one question for you in this regard, which goes as follows: On the basis of your military experience, can you think of any order involving activities which require the use of resources which could be issued by a corps to a brigade, or rather, to one of the assistant commanders of a brigade without first informing the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if the counsel has in mind the security organ in particular, then I can tell you that such a thing can only happen in a situation which would involve counterintelligence tasks and information which would not ask for his departure from the command location or leaving the unit. I don't know whether that was the thing you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I thank you very much for this answer. I don't need any further clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Bourgon. Thank you. Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mitrovic, I'd like us to clarify some of your answers given yesterday to the Prosecutor when you were questioned about the naval military district. Then you said that the then-9th corps, or as you called it, the Knin corps was part of the naval military district of Split. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was while I was with the naval military district.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you know lieutenant-colonel Spiridon Alacov?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Lieutenant-colonel Alacov was an officer who dealt with personnel issues in -- well, I may be mistaken, but I remember him being in the security department of the military naval district.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, Lieutenant-Colonel Spiridon Alacov testified before this Tribunal on the 10th of July, 2008. I will put to you what he said on that occasion. So that the rest could follow Mr. Spiridon's testimony, it can be found at page 23566 from line 2 to line 6. Mr. Spiridon then said that once the war began in Croatia, the Knin corps, i.e., the 9th corps was taken out of the military naval district of Split and put under direct command of the JNA General Staff. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a prisoner at the time, and I was released on the 22nd of November, 1991. I wasn't able to follow what was going on during that time. There may have been such a thing, but I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Another question. In answering my questions about your career, if I recall correctly you said that you were a major at the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When the war ended, you were lieutenant-colonel?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Therefore you were promoted in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When you met Mr. Beara for the first time, what was his rank?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was 1995. He held the rank of naval captain. 1985, sorry. In any case, he also retired holding the same rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Since I'm not a soldier, I'd like to ask you the following: A naval captain would be equivalent to the rank of colonel of the ground forces. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What is your opinion? Do you have any information on why Mr. Beara failed to be promoted?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had there not been for the war -- I may be mistaken, though, but being the head of a security department required a general; therefore, had it not been for the war, he probably would have been promoted to admiral since he was the head of security in the naval military district. As to why he was not promoted, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you recall how -- or rather, what was the rank of Mr. Tolimir when the war broke out and at the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Colonel Tolimir in Knin in 1991 after the exchange there, and at the time he was a colonel. I think he was a major general or lieutenant-general by the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have only one question left. When answering some of the Prosecutor's questions, you explained the decision-making process within the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What you said, was that a textbook example of such a decision being made?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned an example that would be in accordance with the principle as it existed in the army. However, I did say that I am not an expert in the field, but that was the principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge whether things were done differently during the war that people deviated from the principle?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A war is quite a specific -- different situation, and decisions are sometimes made at short notice. Not everything can be put in writing in order to adhere to the procedure. It all depended on the time you have on your hands and, of course, the situation at the frontlines because the enemy simply would not allow you to go through the procedure in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I agree with you in full. Do you have any knowledge of such conditions resulting in the decisions being arrived at through an abbreviated shortened procedure?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such decisions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you relate that to certain events?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at this moment. I cannot recall off the cuff whether such a decision had to be made in that way. Of course, it all depended on the situation at the frontlines. For example, when there was a Muslim breakthrough through our lines in the area of Bihac, I believe, in 1994, then there was no time. We had to use shortcuts and try to re-establish Defence lines, engage units ASAP, and orders were issued verbally. It was an urgent situation, and we had to eliminate the problem as soon as possible in order to stabilised the frontlines, and then we could follow it up with the rest of the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic, I have no further questions, and I believe you have deserved your break. We've given you quite some rough time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. I got the sensation that the witness can survive that. Mr. Mitrovic, unless my colleagues have questions for you, which doesn't seem to be the case, your testimony has reached its end here. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to thank you for having come over and give evidence, and on behalf of everyone I also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to thank you for the fair treatment, in particular during cross-examination by both the Prosecution and Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] None, Your Honours. We've only been using previously tendered exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same, Your Honour. All of the documents we used yesterday are already exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it it's only the Miletic and Gvero Defence teams that wish to tender some documents. Otherwise, if there's someone else, let us know, please. Ms. Fauveau, you have four documents, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The documents that are on the list, 5D1192, 5D1195, and 5D1197 as well as 5D1196 and 97.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: So I'll repeat. 5D1192, 5D1195, 5D1196 and 5D1197.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we object only to the document which is 3516 from the 65 ter list. We have no knowledge of the origin of the document, and we cannot see which organ issued it or who signed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which is 3516? Which one are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Prosecution's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but I was referring to Madam Fauveau's documents? No objection. No objection to Madam Fauveau's exhibits? All right. Thank you. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No objection to the Miletic team exhibits nor to the Gvero team's exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So your exhibits are admitted, Ms. Fauveau. Mr. Krgovic, you have only got one document, which has not yet been translated. At least that's what is stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's Document 6D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. Any objections, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection from anyone else? So this document is also admitted. Your exhibits, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just three, Mr. President, from our exhibit list: 3625, 3659, and 3661.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I would also offer -- typically when I read in portions of a report or transcript, our practice is not to offer the actual pages. Given the length of one of the passages I read, if my friends or if the Trial Chamber thinks it might be more helpful to have a hard copy just in case, I'm happy to put that together as an excerpt just of that one section that was particularly long. If the parties or the Court see no need, then obviously we won't do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Any objections. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm not clear here. 3625 according to the list I've got is the transcript of the witness's interview. I thought that was what my learned friend was just referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I misspoke. That should have been 3659, 3661. My friend is entirely correct. We have no intention of offering the entire interview. I'm just referring to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's not three documents but two?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, it's two documents, Mr. President. I apologise. I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Josse, for your intervention. Do you wish to comment on the offer?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We have no objection to the offer, in other words, the pages that were read out being specifically admitted, if that's of assistance to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. Is there an objection from your part, Mr. Nikolic, or from any other Defence team, for that matter? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. It all depends now on what my colleagues think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The decision is we prefer to have it in the records just in case it becomes necessary later on to understand better the relevant part of the witness's testimony, so it's being admitted, too, only those parts, I mean. I'm not -- none of us is interested in the rest. As to the others, there being no objection, they are also admitted. The point raised by you earlier on, I understand now, is moot because 3615 is not being tendered, Mr. Nikolic, correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please, I just have to check for us if 3659 remains under seal or -- yes. Okay. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Ostojic. I saw you standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Two things: One, we would ask just for a 5- to 7-minute break so we could bring in our binders. There's actually three or so binders that Professor Wagenaar will utilize, and we're changing our staff. There's another young lady who will be assisting me today, so they can disrobe, and if you don't mind giving me those five minutes to do that. The other thing is, I still would like the Court to -- or my learned friends to give us a little more information as to why the documents that we're receiving late that bears our clients name on it were not produced to us other than last week or two weeks ago when they claim it was on the list of exhibits for Mr. Mandic. It's of concern to us. They've had it for over ten years. We've been in this case for quite some time, and I think we've asked them pretty repeatedly to provide such documents, so I just want to have that on the record if nothing else. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think that can be sorted out between yourselves in these seven minutes that we will grant you. There will be a short break of seven minutes approximately, and then we start with the testimony of the new witness. --- Break taken at 4.49 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you ready, Mr. Ostojic? Shall we call in the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And as we are calling the witness in, if I can just, for Mr. President and Your Honours, introduce my assistant today who will be helping us. She's an intern from the Netherlands, and her name is Frederike Ambagtsheer. So I'm just pleased and privileged to have her here with us today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and you are most welcome, madam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For your information, the break will be at the same time as usual, at 5.45. Good afternoon to you, Professor Wagenaar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are most welcome. You've been summoned as witness by the Beara Defence team, but before we proceed with your testimony, in terms of our rules you need to make a solemn declaration that in the course of your testimony you will be testifying the truth. Madam usher is going to hand you the text. Please read it out, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you Professor. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I need to explain to you a preliminary matter, namely that we decided to start with your evidence today, but I assume you have already been told that we won't finish with you today and we will not continue with your evidence tomorrow because we had on our schedule someone else testifying tomorrow, which we can't move, which ultimately means that you will need to return here next week, Monday, to continue. If we don't finish on Monday, then it will spill over onto Tuesday. So that's the position as such. Mr. Ostojic is going to go first. He will introduce himself, and we'll take it up from there then. He will be followed eventually by others on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good evening, Professor. As you know, my name is John Ostojic, and I'm one of the attorneys who represents Ljubisa Beara.
