Sir, before we begin, I'd just like to thank you for accommodating our schedule. It is very much appreciated, and once again, thank you for your understanding. Would you please state your name state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: My name is Willem Albert Wagenaar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Wagenaar, how would you like me to address you today, as Professor as I have in the past or simply as Mr. Wagenaar?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Mr. Wagenaar is all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Sir, can you share with us your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes. I was born the 30th of June, 1941.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In order to have a better idea of you, can you tell us what's the highest level of education that you've attained?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: The highest level of education is that I acquired a PhD in psychology at the University of Leiden.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And when did you accomplish the same?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: That was accomplished in 1972.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And give us a little background of your employment history, and I think you can actually start with what you currently do, and for those of us who are following, I know, Professor, that we have your curriculum vitae marked as 2D560. And the reason I ask and put that to you because I noticed on the last page or the second page of your CV, it does note that it was last updated in May of 2006.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. In 2006, I was employed by the university of Leiden and University of Utrecht both as a professor of experimental psychology and in Leiden, also as a professor of psychology and law. I retired because I reached the age of 65, which is in the Netherlands the age of forced retirement. I retired in June 2006. Since then, I'm officially a retired professor of psychology. I still teach at the University of Utrecht.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, and congratulations on your retirement. Share with us some of your -- or highlight for us some of your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't quite think that he accepts or relishes those congratulations. I don't think he is happy with having been forced. Unfortunately, both the Netherlands and my country have exactly the same situation, which is unfortunate. Let's hope it will change one day, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Professor, can you share with us some of your administrative and advisory positions?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, I've been with my first employer, which is the TNO organisation in the Netherlands, the Organisation For Applied Scientific Research. I was head of the psychology department in my institute. From there on, I went to the University of Leiden where I became the how - do you say it - the chair of psychology; and in 1987, I became the dean of social sciences until 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's also at Leiden University?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Also at Leiden University, and then in 1979 [sic] I became what is called a Rector Magnificus. You might translate it as vice chancellor of Leiden University, which position I had until 2001, so a period -- two terms of two years as we do it in Leiden.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just give us a quick overview of some of the honours that you received throughout your career.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly what you consider to be honours. I was a Fulbright scholar in the year 1973, '74. I became an honourary professor in Holland - you call it university professor; it's really honourary professor - at the University of Utrecht, and I acquired a large number of awards allowing me and my group to do research so awards to which, also, money was connected. I think that those are the most important things. I was appointed special professor at the University of Leuven in Belgium, at the University of Cambridge where I was, as you called it -- and am still an overseas fellow of Churchill College in Cambridge. I am a member of the Royal Academy of Sciences in the Netherlands since 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I see that it's obviously reflected in your CV, which is 2D560, under the section "Honours Received," and that's why I asked you. Sir, let me turn to another topic, and that's publications. Have you written any articles or textbooks?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes. I've written many articles and many textbooks on. Various subjects relevant to the themes that we will be discussing here. Of course, articles and books both in the area of human memory and in the area of psychology and law, which partly is, of course, overlapping because some of my work is on human memory in the context of what happens in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just give us an idea of where your publications can be found and what sources are they actually published in?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: My publications can be found in the normal scientific journals, as in the leading scientific journals in my field, and in several books that are simply available on -- in any book shop, can be ordered through any book shop. My book on problems, psychological problems in the context of the Dutch law is in its 5th edition right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just give us an idea of how many scientific books you've authored.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah, that depends slightly on what you call books, because usually -- see, proceedings and edited books also count as books, but according to some, they don't. But I think altogether there would be a total of ten books or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And how about scientific articles?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Scientific articles, I think that approaches a number of 200 or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, can you share with us, when was the first time that you were contacted by the Beara Defence team in order to provide an analysis and review materials in connection with this case?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I think I was contacted around the beginning of this year while I was still working on another case that was presented to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, we want to -- we are going to spend a lot of time or some significant time talking about memory. On the first page of your report, it actually states that you were contacted in May of 2007. And if you have the report in front of you, I think the Court would also -- would not mind if you use it if necessary.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah, it was not my intention to demonstrate the frailty of human memory, but I cannot also not avoid the fact that human memory is not perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll get into that, I'm sure. So sir, let me restate the question. When was the first time that you were contacted by the Beara Defence team in order to provide your analysis and opinions in connection with this case?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: According to my notes, and these notes, of course, reflect the notes I made in my own diary, that was in May 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you met with me and others from my team, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And can you share with us what the task was that was initially asked of you?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: The task was to -- was actually twofold. First, my first task was to explain to you and also follow that up with a written outline to what the important issues are in the area of recognition and identification by eyewitnesss. That was part one. Part two was to read relevant parts of the case file in this specific case and see how this general knowledge about identification and recognition can be applied to problems that emerge in this case, and so I also wrote a section on what the general knowledge within my discipline means for when it is applied to this specific case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay, and we'll get into your definition of those two terms in a moment, but prior to that, have you testified before in a capacity as an expert witness?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes. My estimate is that I have testified about 1.000 times as expert witness, among which a number of times to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And do you remember how many times you've testified as an expert witness in this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah, although as you can see from my report, is it a matter of definition. I worked on four other cases, but I testified on only in three out of these four because in the last case, the case of Haradinaj, actually, no witnesses were called.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect to the Tadic case that you list in the report, did you -- were you retained as an expert witness for the Prosecution as well as the Defence?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I was approached simultaneously and probably without the two parties being aware of the fact I was approached by both sides to testify, and so I proposed to the Court that I would be try to answer in one report questions from both sides, which, of course, happened to be exactly the same questions, and after some discussion the Court allowed me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what year was that, if you can help us put a time frame on it.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: The case was in 1996. It was, as far as I am aware, the first case that was handled by this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned -- strike that. Before I get into that, what types of cases would you offer expert testimony on in court?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Most of the cases in which I'm asked to testify as an expert concern problems of memory, of human memory, and roughly that can be divided into two specific areas: One is of recognition of people by eyewitnesses, which relies on their visual memory, the remembering faces, usually, and the other section is other problems of eyewitness testimony where they remember facts other than just the faces or the outer appearance of people. So it's usually on either recognition of eyewitnesss or the reliability of their memories about events that they have experienced.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You mentioned both recognition and identification. Do you draw a distinction between the two?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah. I think that needs to be explained. These terms have been introduced with -- there's a very special definition within this Tribunal, and I found it just practical to follow the definitions that have been used by the Tribunal, although I am aware of the fact that within my discipline, the meaning of these words is slightly different, but I don't think it's very useful to confuse the Tribunal by having all sorts of different definitions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And which word are you referring to, sir, "recognition" or "identification," that the Tribunal has set a specific definition for?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Well, both, both have obtained a special definition within this Tribunal, and I think it's -- those definitions can be used very well, are practical, and I will simply follow them. And according to my understanding, the definitions used by this Tribunal are as follows: Recognition is retained for a witness who states that he observed at a moment in history a person whom he knew well, and the witness states, I recognise that person because I knew who that was. The memory task for such a witness is only to remember that he saw a particular person. In fact, the witness only has to remember the name of the person he saw, and remembering the face is easy because he knew that person well and he knows the face of that person. That's recognition.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Identification, as used by this Tribunal, is the witness says he saw a person at the moment in history who at that time he had never seen before. So he met -- he saw that person for the first time in his life. Therefore, in most cases he also did not know who that person was. There's no name to remember. There's only a face or the outer appearance of a person to remember. Later on during investigations, that witness may be asked to look at photographs or videos or lineups or anything to see whether that person is present in those photographs, videos, lineups, and so on. And so the identification task is at that later moment during the investigation. The task for the witness is to remember not a name but to remember the outer appearance of that person, so that requires retaining a visual memory. I myself have always used, as I do in this report, a distinction between familiar people and unfamiliar people. If at the scene of the crime, to simplify it, you see a person that was already familiar to you, then the Tribunal would say you may have recognised that -- that's recognition. If you saw an unfamiliar person, then later on during the investigation there comes a moment of identification, identifying who that person was who you seemed to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: A little more with respect to your background at this point. Have you testified in other Tribunals other than the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes. I've testified for the ICTR in Arusha this year. I have testified in a special Dutch Tribunal for war criminals at the very early moment. I've testified in 1987 in the special Tribunal in Jerusalem set up for the trial of John Demjanjuk who was accused of being a person -- a character called Ivan the Terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And sir, just a little more with respect to definition. On the fourth paragraph of your report, which we have, you seem to -- or at least I think you draw a distinction between perception and memory. Since we're just in the beginning part, I'd like to, perhaps, have a better understanding if, first, you do and then, if you don't mind explaining that for us.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, almost logically, perception precedes memory. If you are a witness, see, the first requirement is that you perceive things. You see them or you hear them, and if you didn't see them or didn't hear them, there's no way that the -- that relevant information could have been stored into your memory. So the first question, always, about a witness is, could the witness see it or could the witness really hear that? The next question is, not only could he see it, but did he see it? Did he pay attention to that because, also, attention is a prerequisite for storing information in your memory. And only if those two answers are positive - yes, it was perceived; yes, attention was paid to it - then it's possible that it was stored into this witness' memory. And from there on, anything that happens is relevant to what the fate of that memory might have been, whether it was retained in memory, the information, or disappeared or was confused or changed and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, earlier when describing the definition or giving us the definition of recognition and identification, you mentioned the two subcategories, as I call them, and forgive me if I'm changing the proper way of calling it, but of a familiar and unfamiliar person. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Does that fall into one specific section under recognition or identification, or is that -- really fall within both those sections or definitions?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: No. When the person whom you saw, say, at the scene of the crime, when the witness claims, I already knew that person before, then the only relevant -- the most relevant question is, was there a good opportunity to recognise that person at the scene of the crime? When the witness states, that was the first time I ever met that person, then the most relevant question -- then there are two relevant questions: Could the witness see this person at the scene of the crime good enough to form a visual image that could be stored into memory; and the next relevant question is, in what way was the witness later on during the investigations asked to identify this person?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, going back to this specific assignment that you received, can you share with us what materials were provided to you or which materials were requested from you to us?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah. I was provided not with the entire case file because that was physically impossible, but I was provided with sections including statements of 12 witnesses, whom I have also listed by number in my report, sections of the statements that related to either recognition or identification. I have no way of checking whether I saw all the relevant sections that are in the case file because I simply could not study the whole case file, but from my report it is at least clear which sections I saw of those statements. Altogether, still, these sections constitute three large binders of information, which I also took to this Court, so it's open to the Court to inspect what actually I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Wagenaar, we actually have brought the binders here just so you have them. If there's a need to refer to them, kindly do so. Just to clarify one issue, when you say "statements," was it actual statements by witnesses that were provided or in-court testimony that was offered during the trial of this case?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah. I think the binders contain two types of information: statements that were taken from them as a preparation of their appearance in Court, but also sections of their actual testimony in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Going back to 1996 and the work that you did for the Prosecution in the Tadic case, give us a little feel, if you will, for what type of work you performed for them at that time. What was the issue at hand?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: In the Tadic case, there were two types of witnesses: Witnesses who claimed that he was a familiar person because they came from the same village and had known him for 10, 20 or even more years; and there were witnesses who said that the first time they saw, allegedly, Mr. Tadic was at the scene of the crime where they saw him committing certain crimes. These witnesses, of course, later were asked to identify the person they saw by means of a photo line-up, and one of my tasks was, of course, to comment on the quality of this photo line-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Was it actually -- and I use a different term and maybe -- I think we are on the same page. Was it a photo board, or was it actually a physical line-up where people would walk across a room with a background that would be considered neutral with height indications, or was it a photo board?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: It was a photo board showing only the faces of people, not their body, so there's nothing you could say about height or build or anything like it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now -- so the Prosecution and you together, obviously, with the Defence attorneys were -- what were you, constructing this photo board?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: No. The photo board had already been constructed and been applied. There was no way for me to influence the actual design of that photo board, the composition, but I did some quantitative research on whether that composition was biased or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just so I understand it better, I think I do, but these photo boards consist of essentially 3-and-a-half-by-5 pictures of individuals who may share the same physical attributes or characteristics, if you will, such as hair, shape of face, eyes, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what you are asking. Are you asking what they should consist of or what they generally consist of?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: First, what they generally consist of. What do they generally consist of?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: They generally consist of pictures presenting people roughly in the same category, like the all white, the all male, or all female. But it cannot be generally said that they always conform to, say, the descriptions that witnesses gave of the person they saw. Sometimes it's quite -- some of the people presented are not fitting those descriptions, which does not make them plausible choice alternatives, and that, then, usually is one of the problems. In the Tadic case, the problem was that all witnesses knew that the accused was -- had a Serbian ethnic background, and the question was, do all the people shown in the line-up, are they also Serbian, or are some of them clearly non-Serbian? So I cannot say generally they all fit the same description. That's usually exactly the topic that needs to be studied.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What is a foil?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: A foil is a person who appears in a photo line-up, in a photo board who fits the same description as the accused but who clearly is innocent and who if identified by the witnesses clearly cannot be suspected of any wrongdoing; and thereby, by that logic, it is shown that the witnesses has not a reliable memory of whom he saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And when -- is there a standard when creating these photo boards?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes. There are good rules, and many countries have adopted such rules, which roughly agree with one another about how these photo boards should be composed and what dangers in the construction of photo boards should be avoided.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And we'll talk about what those rules and standards are. What is a suggestive photo board?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: A suggestive photo board, or we usually call it a biased photo board, is a photo board where what we call a naive person who has never met the accused will, with a much larger likelihood than one out of the number of photos on the board, identify who the accused is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. What would we call that, though, if we just bring a random person in to look at a photo board and give him a short synopsis of who they should identify? Is there a term of art for that?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah. Sure. That test, which you usually run before you show any photo board to real witnesses to make sure that naive witnesses cannot do it, that test is called the test of Doob and Kirshembaum.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you were starting to tell us that were standards that are utilized in creating a photo board, and can you share them with us, please.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I'm obviously asking you for a proper photo board, if you will.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Right. Right. Yeah, and I will try to do it in a succinct manner because in one of my publications I've listed 50 rules for composing photo boards, and I think that's a -- so I will give you a rough indication. What you do is the following: First, you ask the witness to describe the person he saw, and that description defines, then, how all the people in the photo board should look. So all the persons must fit the description given by a specific witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What types of characteristics are normally used?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Usually, the rough categories are male, female, caucasian, Chinese, Japanese, but it can be far more specific; it can also be the distinction between, say, Serbian and Croatian; age, usually witnesses cannot know exactly the age of people, but at least they can mention the age category, like he was middle-aged, he was 30 years, he was an old man; and then facial descriptions like hair-do, facial hair like beards and mustaches; things like scars are important. Those are the most important things. There are also a number of things you should not do. Preferably, a photo board should not show any clothing, or it should show exactly the same clothes on all people. It should, for instance, not show -- if you talk about military people, it should not show insignia because if the rank of a person is known and none of the people in the photo board shows the correct insignia, that would be highly suggestive. They're things like -- we call that clothing bias, and to me that also includes insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You mentioned scars and, obviously, I'm sure tattoos fall in that, if someone would have one on their face. What about things like glasses or other -- piercings someone may have on their face?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah. I think with respect to glasses you should make a distinction to a person usually wearing glasses or maybe even always wearing glasses and people like me who have reading glass who may wear them or may not wear them. But if the witness mentions glasses, then if the accused never wore glasses, you have a problem, and the question is whether you should compose a photo board at all. If you compose a photo board with the accused wearing no glasses, the problem is that actually you inform the witness that he was wrong. He mentioned glasses, but there are no glasses. That's not the purpose of a photo board. The purpose of a photo board is for the witness to inform the investigators, not the other way around. So you have a logical problem there. Obviously, the only correct way of doing it is showing the accused with glasses, his own glasses, and showing all the foils also with glasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we will get into it later during your testimony. Were you informed of us as to whether or not Mr. Ljubisa Beara wore glasses or not in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Whether he wore glasses in 1995. I wasn't informed in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah, I was thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I didn't know you --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes. I saw a number of pictures of Mr. Beara in which he always wear glasses. I've not seen pictures of him without glasses. I have no way of knowing whether he always wore glasses. I can only say that some of the witnesses mentioned glasses, and clearly if there would have been composed any line -ups for those witnesses, but there were not, but if there would have been any form of photo boards, then the accused should have been shown on the photo with his glasses, and all the others should have worn glasses. I also saw that some witnesses whose statements I studied were either uncertain about glasses or did not mention glasses and even in a few cases said, I don't remember glasses or there were no glasses. For these witnesses, if you would use a photo board at all, the only possible way is showing Mr. Beara without glasses, and whether that would be a useful thing to do or not depends on whether Mr. Beara sometimes walks around without glasses or not, and I'm not a judge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Give us a little more detail on the photographs that you reviewed in connection with the issue of glasses and Mr. Beara. Did it range for a time period in his life prior to 1995, or really, because some of them are dated, some are not, was it some periods when he was younger and, obviously, some even after 1995?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah, I saw a number of photographs. I don't have them in my -- all in my possession, but I'm sure you do, showing him from a relatively young man like -- it makes the impression of 30 or so, until -- right until 1995 and even later, I think. In all these pictures, I saw glasses. I have not seen other pictures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just a question, Your Honour. We received for the first time today around 11 o'clock photos of Mr. Beara, and I just want to know if my friend can tell me if what we received today are the same photos which were provided to the witness, if that's what we're talking about, exactly the same photos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll follow up on that, as well, but first, let me ask the professor this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When were you shown the pictures of Mr. Beara that you're discussing here?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Well, I saw a few, maybe two or three pictures last year when I started on the case. A larger number of pictures were shown to me, I think, in the last week when we started to prepare -- when I started to prepare my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And those were all -- because there's a distinction, there were two sets of pictures, one from a video that obviously the Prosecution is shown, witnesses that we gave to Mr. Wagenaar when we gave him the materials, and other pictures that the Prosecution had of Mr. Beara, and then also some family photos that we obtained recently, actually last week, and then shared it with Mr. Wagenaar this week. But those are the ones that we've shown him that are scanned and provided to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you satisfied with that explanation, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: For now, I think so. If I have any questions, I'll ask my friend after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also, for the record, in addition to what previously was stated now, Mr. Elderkin has joined the Prosecution team and is present in the courtroom. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Professor, was there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. In any case, it's time for the break. I don't know if it's convenient for you or whether you wish to proceed with your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's convenient. I mean, it doesn't make a difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Wagenaar and Mr. President, I want to apologise sincerely to you. I didn't hear when you said you were forced into retirement, and I apologise to you and the Court for that, and I answered it, so thank you for that. Now, if I can go back to my question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think he has really retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Forcibly retired from wherever you were mentioning in your background. Sir, we were speaking before the break in reference to glasses, and we'll come back to that topic. Did you notice anything conspicuous about the type of glasses in the photographs that was provided to you initially and then subsequently in connection with either their size, shape, or colour?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: In the photographs that I saw, there were always rather large pairs of glasses so not the type of reading glasses that I'm wearing that are really only half-glasses. They are large -- conspicuously large glasses, but it was very difficult to see on the photograph what type of glasses they were. You could only see that the frame was rather large and conspicuous, always dark, large, conspicuous frames, not the type of invisible frames where you see only glasses. Very clear, dark rims around the glasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, just a couple of other items that I'd like to clear up, and I did speak with my learned friend during the break that we've had, and he had a couple of inquiries of me, and I wasn't able to provide the answers. He wanted to know, because you mentioned the notes that you've taken, do you have and have you maintained notes in connection with that which you've reviewed and analysed with respect to your report and testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: What I did was first review the copies of statements and -- statements by the witnesses and their testimony in these binders. From that, I made together with one of your colleagues a sort of large table with a summary for each witness separately, each of the witness -- where the relevant clauses can be found and what in a very short sentence what they were about. That's what I used to compose the report that was submitted to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that material, you still have that material with you, those synopsis or the short summary that you took from the statements?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether I have them, but I'm sure they can be made available.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If you would be kind enough to make that available to us, and then we'll share it with the Prosecution so they have it as well.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With respect to -- you mentioned also during the first 45 minutes of your testimony, when we generally spoke of rules in connection with both recognition and identification that these were universally or widely accepted rules, and you said in many countries, and I failed to follow-up, in which countries are these types of rules that you're discussing with us, today universally accepted?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I mentioned as examples the United Kingdom where the so-called PACE rules have been adopted as standard; I mentioned the United States where a very clear set of rules that can also be downloaded from the internet is used; and I mentioned my own country, the Netherlands, where a set of rules has been published and adopted in the year 2002 by our Minister of Justice as the standard that must be used by the Office of the public -- Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And why the Office of the Prosecutor, though? Do you know why are these rules actually those that the Prosecution should abide by?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Well, I think that there's a technical reason. The Minister of Justice has only authority over the Office of the Prosecutor, not over the Defence, and not at all over the Judges, so the Minister of Justice can only prescribe it to the Prosecutor that evidence to be presented in court by the Prosecutor should conform to the standards.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are these rules universally known to criminal investigators?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, I would say so, that any criminal investigator should as a professional know how line -ups are to be organised, and I would be very surprised if a professional criminal investigator had never used of those. On the contrary, as a custom I would say an experienced criminal investigator has in his or her lifetime used these procedures more than once.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that the rules can be found on the internet or the computer. Are they easily accessible?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: They are easily accessible. You just -- you just -- if you Google PACE rules or anything like that, "US identification rules," you just find them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know from your experience in testifying at this Tribunal and in other cases as well as this one, do you know if these rules that we're going to discuss were known to the ICTY investigators from the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: No. In the context of this specific case, I've received not so much information about the investigators and what they know and neither of identification rules adopted by this Tribunal. I know from previous cases that there is at least a summary statement of the Tribunal about how identifications are to be done. These statements are rather short, I would say, and not as extensive as one would want them to be because many aspects that are usually adopted in such rules are missing here, and I've commented on it before. But in principle, I would hope that investigators delegated to ICTY by various member states of the United Nations would be experienced people who are aware of, say, the common practice in the world and could apply them even without very specific directions from ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. How about whether you know whether OTP investigators in previous cases used this line-up test or, as I call it, photo board. You call it a photo line-up. I am assuming it's interchangeable, but you correct me if I'm wrong. Do you know if they've used this in prior cases?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes. In the cases of Tadic, they were used, as we already discussed. In the case in which I testified, the case of Prosecutor versus Kupreskic, it wasn't relevant because Kupreskic recorded seeing a person well known to him, his own neighbour. In the case of Prosecutor versus Limaj were extensive photo boards or photo line -ups used, and in the case of Prosecutor versus Haradinaj in which I finally did not testify because no witnesses were asked to testify at all by the Defence, there were also photo boards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you proceed. Professor, is there any difference in approach between -- to your knowledge between civil law countries and common-law countries on these standards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The standards are exactly the same because, in principle, the foundation of those standards are within my discipline and not -- actually are not derived from legal principles. They are derived from the methods for psychological testing, and they are completely independent of, say, the type of law that is used within a particular country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And one further question. Is there any either regional or global association whereby experts like you on this subject meet and discuss regularly and update yourselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. There is, for instance, in Europe the European Psychology and Law Association. They had their last international meeting in -- last summer in Maastricht, and there were many reports on identification procedures, and I, also, myself reported on identification there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it you are a member of that association.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Wagenaar, with respect to this case, from the materials that you reviewed were you able to determine whether a photo board was done in connection with any of the accused?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I'm only aware of a photo board that I've seen that was used in relation to the accused Mr. Popovic, but I did not review extensively the sections of the case file that relate to this particular accused, so I can only report to you that I saw this line-up, but I have further no opinions about the quality or the adequacy of that line-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I'm not going to ask you about that. But just so that we have it for the record, and I'd like to go into private session. I told you, Professor, we may do that from time to time in order to protect the identity of some of the individuals who have testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And with the Court's permission, I'd like to go into private session for just it this one short --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. By all means. Let's go into private session now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you have an opinion as to whether or not the OTP and the Prosecutors there knew how to prepare at least a photo board, whether proper or not, and I'm not asking you to pass -- give us or share with us any opinion in connection with that photo board because you were not retained to do that, but do you know if they -- by looking at some of this and your knowledge in other cases, did they have the knowledge and the know-how to prepare a photo board?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'm going to object to the form of the question. He can't answer what was in the knowledge and know-how. I think he rephrase that simply and make an analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Ostojic, you can adapt yourself to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'll do it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Wagenaar, do you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Especially since you yourself told him that he was not retained to --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, whether or not the Prosecution had the capacity or the capability to prepare a photo identification board such as the one that we've seen in closed session, 2D571?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because if it exists and we have seen it, then obviously the Prosecution had the facility...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I agree they did, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And from other cases as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC

utterances.text: Yeah. The rules as I described them are based on psychological testing methods that are designed to ensure valid outcomes, outcomes that can be relied upon. So one argument for using those rules is that they're based on the logic of psychological testing, and a recognition test is a psychological test. Another area to look at is at evaluation studies, of outcomes of investigations especially in cases where judicial error could be demonstrated because of later DNA analyses, and by now, the literature reviews over 200 of such cases. And one important publication in that area is by Gross and others in 2003. It is so important because it has the largest number of cases reviewed at any time, in 2004, I must say. It's called Exonerations in the United States, 1989 through 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Post-event information is information the witness receives after witnessing the event on which he will testify so that his memory to that event is not only based on what he actually witnessed but partly also on what other information he obtained later on. The problem of that is that this is not harmful if the witness can make a clear distinction between what he actually witnessed and what he was informed about later on. The problem, though, is that witnesses find that in many cases very difficult and will report some information they received later as information they actually witnessed themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR
utterances.text: A multiperson identification test is what we have referred to as a photo board where the witness actually is asked to look at the number of people of which one is the accused and the others are innocent foils, and the witness is asked to tell whether the person he described before is present in the photo board at all, and if so, to point out which picture or which person that is where the instruction clearly is there can either be one of such people or none. You can point at only one, and you have to make a selection from the whole photo board. The rationale of having a sufficient some of others, of foils there, is that you would like to reduce the likelihood that just by guessing you happen to point out the one person who is the accused, so therefore, you need a larger number of foils there, usually we say at least five foils, preferably something like ten foils or something.
